passage: At nursery, Kiran, four, kept tickling Baljeet's neck during story time. "Stop, I don't like that," said Baljeet, raising her hand. Kiran laughed and did it again. Baljeet looked at the teacher. "Miss, he won't stop." The teacher knelt beside her. "Thank you for telling me. Kiran, when a friend says stop, we stop." Kiran moved back. "Are you okay, Baljeet?" She nodded and leaned forward for the story.

qa.q: What did Baljeet say to Kiran?
qa.a: "Stop, I don't like that."

qa.q: What was Baljeet likely feeling when Kiran did it again?
qa.a: Annoyed and uncomfortable, perhaps a little helpless, which may be why she told the teacher. Kiran might have thought it was a game.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that showed the report mattered?
qa.a: She thanked Baljeet, told Kiran to stop when a friend says stop, and checked that Baljeet was okay.

qa.q: How might Kiran see the tickling?
qa.a: As a fun game, since he laughed. He may not have understood it upset Baljeet until the teacher explained.

grounding: Shows a preschooler saying stop and telling a trusted adult when it continues, with a calm, serious response.

passage: I'm Nazia, and I watched my little sister Shreya, five, at a birthday party. A man I had only just met tried to lift her up. "Stop, I don't want that," Shreya said, loud and clear, stepping back. He laughed it off and reached again. She ran across the room to our mother. "He won't stop." Mum went straight over, calm, took Shreya onto her lap and said, "Thank you for telling me." I don't know exactly what Shreya felt, but she did what she had been taught.

qa.q: Who did Shreya run to when he reached again?
qa.a: Their mother, across the room.

qa.q: How might Shreya have felt when the man reached for her again?
qa.a: Uncomfortable and perhaps scared, shown by stepping back and running to her mother. The man may have meant it as playful.

qa.q: What did Nazia's mother do that supported Shreya?
qa.a: She went straight over calmly, took Shreya onto her lap and thanked her for telling.

qa.q: How does Nazia see Shreya's reaction?
qa.a: She is unsure exactly what Shreya felt but sees that Shreya spoke up and went to a trusted adult, as she had been taught.

grounding: Shows a preschooler saying stop and telling her mother when someone will not stop, seen by an older sister.

passage:
Saturday: Ankita's older cousin Lalit tickled her on the sofa. She laughed, then gasped, “Stop! I don't like that!” Lalit kept going. She wriggled free, face red. That evening she told her mother, “Lalit didn't stop when I said stop.” Her mother put down her phone and listened. “Thank you for telling me. You were right to say stop.” She went straight to Lalit and told him calmly, “When someone says stop, you stop. Every time.”
Sunday: Lalit tickled her toes. “Stop,” Ankita said. He stopped at once.
Next Saturday: They played tickle-tag, and both kept the stop rule.

qa.q: What did Ankita say when Lalit tickled her?
qa.a: “Stop! I don't like that!”

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when she wriggled free with a red face?
qa.a: She was upset and uncomfortable, and probably angry that her stop was ignored.

qa.q: What did Ankita's mother do that a trusted adult should do?
qa.a: She listened calmly, thanked Ankita, said she was right, and spoke to Lalit that same evening.

qa.q: How might Lalit see the tickling after the talk?
qa.a: He learns that stop means stop, even in play, which is why he stops at once on Sunday.

grounding: A preschooler says stop when tickling goes too far, tells her mother when it doesn't stop, and her mother acts calmly the same day.

passage: The school picnic by the lake was crowded and noisy, and the buses were leaving in half an hour. A big boy kept tugging at Tejas's shorts as a joke. Tejas said, “Stop, I don't like that.” The boy laughed and did it again. Tejas ran to Uma Ma'am. “He won't stop pulling my shorts.” Uma put down the snack boxes at once. “Thank you for telling me. You did the right thing.” She called the boy over, told him firmly it stops now, and wrote a note to both families that evening.

qa.q: What did the big boy keep doing?
qa.a: Tugging at Tejas's shorts as a joke.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when he ran to Uma Ma'am?
qa.a: He was upset and uncomfortable, and probably embarrassed, because the boy ignored his stop.

qa.q: What did Uma Ma'am do, even in a rush?
qa.a: She put everything down, thanked Tejas, spoke firmly to the boy at once, and wrote to both families that evening.

qa.q: How might the big boy see it after Uma spoke?
qa.a: He might realise that his joke wasn't funny to Tejas and that stop must be respected.

grounding: A preschooler says stop, then tells his teacher when a boy won't stop, and she takes it seriously the same day.

passage: In their flat, Gurleen and Pooja practised a game. Gurleen poked Pooja's arm gently. Pooja held up her hand. “Stop, I don't like that!” “Great voice. And if someone doesn't stop?” “I tell you, or Ma'am.” Two days later at the colony park, a girl kept pinching Pooja's arm. Pooja held up her hand. “Stop, I don't like that!” The girl kept on. Pooja ran to Gurleen on the bench. Gurleen listened, thanked her, and went with her at once to speak to the girl and her mother.

qa.q: What did Pooja do with her hand when she said stop?
qa.a: She held it up.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling when she ran to Gurleen?
qa.a: She was probably upset and a bit hurt that the girl kept pinching, but also confident enough to use her words and tell.

qa.q: Why was the practice game useful?
qa.a: It gave Pooja the words and the plan to tell a trusted adult, so she knew what to do when it really happened.

qa.q: How might the girl's mother react when Gurleen speaks to her?
qa.a: She would likely take it seriously and talk to her daughter about stopping when someone says stop.

grounding: A preschooler practises saying stop, uses it at the park, tells her mother when it doesn't work, and her mother acts calmly at once.

passage:
"Mama, Rehaan keeps squeezing my cheeks. I said stop, I don't like that. He won't stop."

Anjali put down her phone and turned fully towards Dilnaz. "You said stop, and he didn't?"

"He laughed and did it again. It hurts."

"Thank you for telling me. You did exactly the right thing." Anjali stood up. "Let's go and talk to Rehaan now."

In the courtyard, Anjali said calmly, "Rehaan, when Dilnaz says stop, you stop. Every time."

Rehaan went red. "I was only playing."

"She said stop. Then the game is over."

"Sorry, Dilnaz."

qa.q: What did Rehaan keep doing to Dilnaz?
qa.a: He kept squeezing her cheeks.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling when she told her mother?
qa.a: She was most likely upset and hurt, because Rehaan ignored her "stop" and laughed. Telling her mother shows she trusted Anjali to help.

qa.q: What did Anjali do that showed she took the report seriously?
qa.a: She put her phone down, listened, thanked Dilnaz and went straight to talk to Rehaan the same moment, calmly making the rule clear.

qa.q: How does Rehaan see the cheek-squeezing at first?
qa.a: He thinks it is only playing, and goes red when Anjali explains that once Dilnaz says stop, the game is over.

grounding: It shows a preschooler saying stop and then telling a trusted adult when her cousin won't stop, and the adult responding calmly and at once.
